cells.tense: You are here with your hands on the work, tending what is growing, and the tending is your own.
cells.ask: Offer one thing you've been carrying alone a place in someone else's hands, not to hand it off but to let it be seen.
cells.core:
You're the one keeping the garden, and you know it. You decide what gets water and what gets pulled, and you do it without making a show of it. The pull toward what you want is still pulling, and it has become something you care for in daylight — steady, unforced, plainly yours. The plants come up because you showed up for them, and you'd say so if asked.

A garden grows best when the work of growing it is noticed, not only the harvest. Let someone see the tending itself, the early mornings nobody was there for. What arrives then is not praise. It is weight set down, and setting it down is the reward for having carried it well.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what matters, and the caring is steady.
cells.verb: Tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: Standing where the pull of what you want is felt — the direction you steer by

cells.tense: You are already in next season, planning for a harvest that hasn't been planted yet.
cells.ask: Let one imagined outcome rest unmanaged for a day, and let what you have actually built speak for itself.
cells.core:
Tending this well looks like knowing what to leave alone — checking the soil, seeing what's alive, resisting the urge to add another row because there's room. When it's working, the caring has a rest in it. You water what's there and let the season do the rest.

You're keeping six gardens at once, and every one of them is in your head before it's in the ground. The care is real, but it has become a bracing — tending futures that haven't arrived, which leaves nothing in your hands for the one that is here. What goes wrong is the timing, not the wish.

The dream does not need defending. It needs to be allowed to have been enough. Let what you already tend be what it is, without adding another row. Ease is what comes back when the doing stops outstripping the having.
cells.sheetLine: You're farming the future and the present is going untended.

cells.tense: You stopped at a gate some time back and your hands are still resting on it, not pushing.
cells.ask: Make one small, tangible improvement to something that is already growing, without looking for the result.
cells.core:
Tending this well is a plain thing — noticing what's dry and giving it water, checking what's thriving and leaving it be. When it's working, the caring is quiet and regular. The hands know the work and don't need to think about it.

You know how to tend things — you did it long enough that it used to be second nature — but somewhere you set the watering can down and haven't picked it up again. The pull toward what you want is still there, still pointed, but the doing of it has gone quiet.

Tending doesn't need a grand return. It needs one hand on one thing that is alive and wants to keep living. The strength that comes back is not a harvest. It is the knowledge that your hands still remember the work.

cells.tense: You are already shaping what grows, and you describe it as though the shaping were happening on its own.
cells.ask: Tell one person plainly what you have been quietly keeping alive, and let them answer.
cells.core:
You are in the middle of the garden you planted, doing work that matters, and you keep speaking of it as though the garden tended itself. The care is running perfectly — what has gone missing is the claiming of it. You are not watching this happen. You are the one making it happen.

The one who tends it is the one who gets to say so. Not the person who benefits, not the person who happened to be standing nearby, not the weather. You have been watering this all along. Say that out loud, in your own voice, and let it be true in someone else's hearing.
